title: The Scramble for Africa
summary: Why European powers raced to colonise Africa in the late 1800s, the Berlin Conference, how Africa was divided, and how Africans resisted.

notes.text: What was the Scramble for Africa?

In **1870** Europeans controlled only about 10% of Africa, mostly along the coast. By **1914** they controlled about **90%**; only **Ethiopia** and **Liberia** remained independent. This rapid race by European powers to take over African land is called the **Scramble for Africa**.
When a powerful country takes control of another territory and its people, rules them and uses the land and resources for its own benefit.
The policy of extending a country's power and influence by gaining colonies or controlling other countries.

rows: Industrial Europe needed raw materials (rubber, cotton, palm oil, copper, gold) and new markets to sell factory goods
Colonies brought prestige and power; rivals Britain, France and Germany each wanted more land than the others
Control of sea routes, ports and the Suez Canal (opened 1869)
Missionaries wanted to spread Christianity; many Europeans held racist ideas that they were 'civilising' Africans
Quinine (against malaria), steamships, railways, the telegraph and the **Maxim gun** made conquest possible

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: Europeans often said they were bringing 'civilisation, commerce and Christianity'. Historians point out that the main motive was economic gain, and that these ideas were used to justify taking African land.

notes.title: Sorting the motives
notes.problem: Sort these into economic, political or religious motives: raw materials for factories; national prestige; converting people to Christianity.
steps: Prestige and power over rivals are **political**.
notes.answer: Economic, political and religious, in that order.

notes.text: To avoid war between themselves, 14 countries met in **Berlin**, hosted by German Chancellor **Otto von Bismarck**. **No Africans were invited.** They agreed on rules for claiming African territory:

items: A country had to inform the others of its claims.
It had to show **effective occupation**: officials, soldiers or traders on the ground.
King Leopold II of Belgium was recognised as owner of the **Congo Free State**.
Free trade and navigation were promised on the Congo and Niger rivers.

notes.text: Borders were drawn with rulers on maps, often as straight lines, without regard for the people living there. Some ethnic groups were split between colonies, while rival groups were forced together. Many of these borders remain today and have caused conflicts after independence.

notes.caption: Main colonial powers by 1914
rows: Egypt, Nigeria, Gold Coast (Ghana), Kenya, Rhodesia, South Africa
Algeria, Senegal, Mali, Madagascar, most of West Africa
German South West Africa (Namibia), Tanganyika, Cameroon, Togo

items: **Battle of Adwa (1896)**: Emperor **Menelik II** of Ethiopia defeated the Italian army and kept Ethiopia independent.
**Herero and Nama** in German South West Africa rose up in 1904; the Germans responded with genocide, killing about 80% of the Herero.
**Maji Maji rebellion** (1905–1907) in German East Africa.
**Asante** (Ashanti) wars against the British in the Gold Coast, including Yaa Asantewaa's war (1900).
**Battle of Isandlwana (1879)**: the Zulu army defeated the British, although the Zulu kingdom was conquered later that year.

notes.title: Why was Ethiopia able to win at Adwa?
notes.problem: Explain how Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896.
steps: Emperor Menelik II had bought modern rifles.
He united a very large army.
Italian forces were outnumbered and poorly co-ordinated in unfamiliar terrain.
notes.answer: Modern weapons, unity and numbers let Ethiopia stay independent.
